lesson.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specAnchors.text: understand the basic principles of a mass spectrometer and be able to analyse and interpret mass spectra to: i deduce the isotopic composition of a sample of an element ii calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from relative abundances of isotopes and vice versa iii determine the relative molecular mass of a molecule, and hence identify molecules in a sample iv understand that ions in a mass spectrometer may have a 2+ charge
be able to predict mass spectra, including relative peak heights, for diatomic molecules, including chlorine, given the isotopic abundances

primer.text: The mass spectrometer is the census-taker of isotopes. This note follows a sample through ionisation, acceleration, deflection and detection, averages isotope abundances into relative atomic masses, extends the technique to molecular ions and the carbon-13 M+1 satellite, and predicts the telltale halogen doublets and triplets.

modules.title: Reading a mass spectrum of an element
modules.opening: The mass spectrometer is the instrument that finds what balances cannot: the mass and abundance of each isotope. This lesson walks a sample through vaporisation, ionisation, acceleration, deflection and detection, then reads the spectrum the detector prints.
keyPoints: A mass spectrometer determines relative isotopic masses and their relative abundances.
Electron bombardment vaporises the sample and knocks electrons out, making positive ions.
Electromagnets in the flight tube deflect ions by their mass-to-charge ratio.
Every detector strike is recorded as a small current and amplified into a peak.

low.restatement: The machine turns atoms into positive ions, bends their paths by mass, and counts how many of each mass arrive.
low.analogy: It is a sorting chute for ions: heavier loads curve less and land at their own bin, each hit ringing the bell.
low.examPointer: Sequence marks come from naming the five stages in order.

medium.restatement: Ionisation converts neutral atoms into charged particles so fields can act on them; varying the magnetic field sweeps every mass-to-charge ratio across the detector, and abundance follows from strike frequency.
medium.analogy: Charging the balls is what lets the magnet sort them - uncharged marbles ignore the field entirely.
medium.examPointer: Applications beyond isotopes - drug detection, forensics, space probes and carbon dating - earn naming marks.

modules.title: From abundances to relative atomic mass
modules.opening: A spectrum is a census of isotopes, and the census averages into the periodic table's Ar values. This lesson applies the weighted-mean equation to oxygen and boron spectra, then extends the technique to molecular ions and the M+1 carbon-13 peak.
keyPoints: Isotopes are same-element atoms with equal protons but different neutron counts.
Ar = (abundance x mass summed over isotopes) / 100.
The molecular ion (M+) peak's m/z equals the compound's relative molecular mass; the M+1 peak grows with carbon count.

low.restatement: Multiply each isotope's mass by its abundance, add them up, divide by 100 - that weighted average is the Ar.
low.analogy: It is a class average where each isotope's mark is weighted by how many students (atoms) earned it.
low.examPointer: Read abundances straight off the peak heights when a spectrum is drawn.

medium.restatement: The weighted mean converts an isotopic mixture into one effective mass per atom; for molecules, the M+ peak reports the molecular mass while the M+1 satellite reports carbon-13's natural abundance, scaling with carbon count.
medium.analogy: The M+ peak is the molecule's weight, and the M+1 peak is the shadow it casts because one carbon in a hundred is heavier.
medium.examPointer: m/z 58 identifies propanal over butanal (72) - molecular-ion peaks distinguish candidates.

modules.title: Predicting halogen doublets
modules.opening: Chlorine and bromine wear their isotopes openly, printing unmistakable peak patterns into molecular spectra. This lesson builds the 3:1, 9:6:1, 1:1 and 1:2:1 patterns from probability and reads them as element detectors.
keyPoints: Chlorine: 35Cl and 37Cl in 3:1 ratio give M : M+2 peaks at 3:1 for one Cl atom.
Two chlorine atoms give three peaks in 9:6:1 ratio from (3/4, 1/4) pairing.
Bromine: 79Br and 81Br in 1:1 ratio give equal M and M+2 peaks for one Br atom.
Two bromine atoms give a 1:2:1 triplet; halogens are therefore visible in spectra.

low.restatement: One chlorine atom splits a molecular ion into a 3:1 doublet; one bromine atom makes an even 1:1 doublet.
low.analogy: The halogen tag is like a barcode printed on the spectrum: count the bars and you know which halogen and how many atoms.
low.examPointer: Quote the abundance ratio (3:1 or 1:1) before quoting peak ratios - the logic marks live there.

medium.restatement: Each halogen atom contributes an independent 3/4-1/4 (chlorine) or 1/2-1/2 (bromine) probability, so two atoms multiply: (3/4)^2 : 2(3/4)(1/4) : (1/4)^2 = 9:6:1 for chlorine and 1:2:1 for bromine.
medium.analogy: It is coin-toss arithmetic: two coins make HH, HT+TH, HT patterns with 1:2:1 counts - bromine is a fair coin, chlorine a biased one.
medium.examPointer: The M+2 peak's doubled weight for mixed isotopes (two ways to make 35-37) is the step examiners watch for.

glossary.definition: The mass of one isotope relative to carbon-12, measured by the mass spectrometer.
The percentage share of an isotope in a natural sample, read from peak heights.
The whole molecule with one electron removed, whose m/z equals the relative molecular mass.
The satellite peak from carbon-13's natural abundance, growing with the molecule's carbon count.

workedExample.prompt: Boron's mass spectrum shows peaks at m/z 10 (19.9%) and m/z 11 (80.1%). Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron to 1 dp.
